text: Meghan Sullivan: It strikes me, as somebody who's a huge space --
Ariel Ekblaw: Nerd.
MS: Fangirl is what I would say,
is that having these really concrete and ambitious goals,
like going to the moon or putting people on the space station,
sometimes forces us to focus our attention on solving problems
that then help us solve problems back here on earth.
AE: This is exactly what we want to do in space.
[Intersections]
[Ariel Ekblaw, Space architect]
[Meghan Sullivan, Philosopher]
AE: Off we go.
What does the common good actually mean
and how do we build towards it?
MS: I think a lot of people assume that the common good means
finding the kind of least common denominator that we can agree on,
like just splitting the difference
or kind of, finding like, going down to the basics.
I think that is a huge mistake.
The philosophers that I study and love, the ancient Greeks, like Aristotle,
believe that the common good, the good itself,
is something that you're moving towards.
It's a common goal and nobody is there yet.
So when we talk about prioritizing the common good,
I think we're not trying to figure out,
of all the things that we believe and care about now,
how do we sort of settle --
AE: And figure out what we already share.
MS: Exactly.
Instead, we need to be having this conversation
of where do we collectively want to move to,
which presumably is very different from where we currently are,
which is probably not that great.
AE: I think this is really compelling.
In our field for space, we think about the space commons
and try to define what is the public good
in the context of a really broad geographical expanse,
like the near-Earth cocoon of space.
And we don't have a real space commons yet.
It does exist as a space,
but we haven't defined all the norms yet.
And so I love this,
this is a way that we can think about moving together
towards the definition of maybe a future goal.
An aspirational version of humanity's commons.
MS: And maybe trying to figure out
what it means to be an interplanetary species.
We might imagine, like, exercise our imagination
about how to be a better planetary species in the process.
AE: Love that.
MS: Alright.
What do we owe each other as humans?
AE: Hmm.
I think we should owe each other the alternative to the Hobbesian view.
The idea that human nature is fundamentally wrought at its base,
or somehow pegged to our lowest basis instinct.
I think we should owe each other our highest version of ourselves
or our more honorable version of ourselves.
MS: Oh, I like that.
So you disagree with Hobbes
that life should be nasty, brutish, and short.
That's pretty, pretty depressing.
AE: It should be elevated, you know, delightful and long.
MS: One of my favorite 20th-century philosophers
is [a] philosopher named Iris Murdoch.
And she has a good answer to this question.
She says, what we owe another person is to be willing to look at them again.
Which means like, oftentimes we meet people,
and we form our assumptions and stereotypes about them.
We put them in a little category in our brain,
and then we interact with them according to that category.
AE: We put them in a box too early.
MS: Oh my gosh.
And she's like, 80 percent of the time,
your first impression is pretty dumb.
AE: This is something I have learned in my life.
I think for the last 10 years,
I thought I was great at first impressions
and then judging people in a positive sense,
but quickly and decisively.
And I think I have learned recently
that I really do need to give people a second look.
I love this comment.
MS: And just being able to like, say, alright, I've got a vibe on you.
I'm going to just put this on the shelf and just take it --
And she's like, really look at the person.
Just make yourself see like, there's a person there.
So I think if we did that, maybe things would start to go better.
AE: That was a great toss.
If you could design a better world for humans from scratch,
what's the first rule?
MS: You know, I come at philosophy from a Catholic perspective.
And in the Jewish tradition and the Christian tradition,
there was a fundamental rule that was laid down at the beginning
that then we just promptly disregarded,
which is you will love your neighbor as another self, like, as yourself,
like, you're going to put love
at the basis of all the rest of your decision making.
And pretty much as soon
as that kind of fundamental operating principle was laid down,
we all started ignoring it and like, revising it.
So I don't know if I would revise the original code,
but I would maybe enforce it a little bit harder.
I don't know if that's allowed as an answer.
What would you do?
AE: I think in the context of space environments,
we're often in isolated, confined environments,
tiny, constrained little spaces.
So if I was going to start with a new rule for humanity,
I love the idea of an oldie but goodie,
the golden rule: treat others how you would like to be treated.
And I think that that actually would play out very well
in a constrained space where what goes around comes around,
all happens very quickly,
with kind of a small, you know, proto group of humans in a space habitat.
It's like almost a tiny little, maybe not a civilization,
but a tiny little society in its own right.
So yeah, something like recommitting to the golden rule
and this sense of really treating other people
in the way in which you would like to be received and seen and treated.
MS: I love it.
You're going to love this one.
What is a hope you have for humans in the next ten years?
AE: I have an aspiration for humans:
that more people get to experience the overview effect,
which really means democratizing access to space
so that more humans can fly up to low-Earth orbit,
look back down at the Earth and see the Earth from space.
And even really serious military astronauts,
very, you know, impeccably well-trained, brave people,
they start to cry when they see the Earth from space.
They lose control over their own emotions because it is so moving.
And I would love to share that experience with more people.
That's a hope I would have.
MS: I think, on my end, similar hope --
that we’d have a kind of realization,
I'm very excited about the AI decade finally taking root.
And I consider myself kind of pragmatic optimist about artificial intelligence.
But my biggest hope
is that we would use this powerful technology
that we now have at our disposal
to help a whole lot more folks realize what it means to be genuinely human,
that like, kind of humans be the star.
It heightens the difference,
and also, there's so much about our lives pre-AI
that [is] dehumanizing,
so many ways in which we learn, in which we work,
that have never enabled us
to really express what's special about being a human being.
I'd love to think that now we have this technology,
we would choose to develop it in a way where humans,
and our capabilities and virtues would be the star of the show.
I don't know that that's going to happen.
I'm kind of afraid it's not,
but maybe if we had the chance
to see where we stand in the perspective of the universe,
it would go better.
AE: What is the biggest barrier to human thriving?
MS: The biggest barrier to human thriving?
There are some really big barriers,
but I think probably the biggest one is our inattention.
You know, we're rational animals,
we have extraordinarily great capabilities in us,
but the only way that we realize them, unlike most animals,
which kind of mature and develop their powers no matter what,
a squirrel becomes a good squirrel with very little effort.
Humans require a great deal of effort
to become good versions of what we're supposed to be,
and [that] requires a lot of attention, not just to ourselves,
but attention on the part of our parents and teachers.
And I think when we fail to flourish,
it's not typically because we've had some malicious plan
that's screwed up our lives.
But really, we just never had the opportunity
to focus on the good plan.
So I would think distraction.
How about you?
AE: That's a great response.
Like, we are really high-intensity creatures
in the sense we need a lot of attention.
We need a lot of explicit care and development
to become maybe the best version of ourselves.
For me, it's interesting.
I think of this sometimes in the context
of why do we spend so much money on space exploration
if some of the barriers to human thriving
are things like poverty,
war, climate change,
there's a lot of things at a societal scale
that might be keeping us from thriving in the way that we really could.
And then there arises the question,
why would we spend money on space at all in that context.
And I think one of the things we could do to help human thriving
is we can use space for the benefit of life on Earth.
So before we go [and] be a sci-fi spacefaring species,
maybe we earn our right to go do that someday
by showing that we can take really good care
of our own planet first.
So try to do things in space that would help with human thriving.
And my latest favorite one is biology.
It turns out biology is really different when you're floating in orbit
than when you're on the ground.
And so we might be able to do things like cancer cures,
Alzheimer's, organoids, testing,
all kinds of interesting things that would maybe help humans thrive
in a more concrete, immediate way on Earth,
but leveraging space technology.
MS: It strikes me as somebody who's a huge space --
AE: Nerd?
MS: Fangirl is what I would say,
is that having these really concrete and ambitious goals,
like going to the moon or putting people on the space station
sometimes forces us to focus our attention
on solving problems that then help us solve problems back here on earth.
And having a big vision like that,
sometimes [is] exactly the kick in the pants you need
to feel motivated to take on something that in your ordinary life
might not feel like it deserves your attention.
AE: This is exactly what we want to do in space.
Producer: Nice.
MS: How do we build systems that influence the good in each other?
AE: Systems that influence the good in each other
also have to assume good intentions at the base.
And so being able to think about what is the architecture of policy
that comes out of the US government,
or ways that we could unify people to get them there.
And I've recently become really passionate
about something completely outside of my domain,
so maybe I'm a little over my skis,
which is an idea of a national service, not necessarily a military draft.
My parents are both ex-military -- I’m very supportive of the military,
but something that would be like
every young person does something for a year when they're 18.
And it really unites red and blue-state kids
and urban and rural kids.
And it could be Teach for America --
it could be something that's service-oriented.
Also, maybe, military service-oriented,
but something like that I think.
Once you get to know the people of your community and your village
and your society and your civilization a little bit better,
I think you can do a better job of finding the good in them
and then maybe building good systems around them.
MS: I love that.
I think on my end, there are a few institutions
that really roll up their sleeves
and do this work of forming people's characters.
One is education,
another would be, like, church and religious organizations.
And a third is the media.
And everybody likes to like, talk about how awful, you know,
whatever, fill in the blank social media is,
but, you know, genuinely print media,
the news and various sources still very much form people’s outlook
and what they hope for
and what they view as their sort of purpose in life.
And I think we have sorely neglected those institutions,
and a lot of people are really on the brink of nihilism
... right now
about whether we could still imagine amazing schools,
whether we could still imagine on the weekends,
you going and being with other humans
and doing some kind of collective activity.
And I think if we really want to design systems
that will bring out the good in people,
we've got to recognize that we are social animals
and that these human-level institutions need to remain strong
and need our investment and our attending.
So I would love to see just, you know,
a renaissance of hope in what we're able to build
in those kinds of institutions.
AE: I love this and just reinvesting in bringing humans together
through these different institutions
in the ways that we used to come together and convene
and gather more, religious and non-religious.
I would love to do that with you, let's start it.
MS: Let's do it.
AE: Thank you so much.
It was a delight talking to you and learning more about your work.
MS: I had so much fun.
